appraisal_events.evidence: « Bathilde ! viens donc empêcher ton mari de boire du cognac ! » ... ma grand'mère repartait, triste, découragée ... sa faiblesse, vaincue d'avance
appraisal_events.explanation: The family (instigated by the great-aunt) teases the grandmother by provoking her husband to drink against his diet, so her heartfelt pleas are futile and she is left sorrowful and defeated; the narrator explicitly frames this as a real persecution he found horrifying, not a comic aside.

appraisal_events.evidence: ceux où il y avait du monde à dîner et où, à cause de cela, elle ne montait pas me dire bonsoir. Le monde se bornait habituellement à Swann
appraisal_events.explanation: On evenings with a guest (typically Swann), the mother does not come up to kiss the narrator goodnight, excluding the child from a ritual he depends on for comfort.

status_effects.explanation: Her pleas to her husband are disregarded and the family's teasing leaves her defeated and sorrowful within this local scene, even though the narrator's sympathy remains fully with her.
The presence of company (usually Swann) locally excludes the narrator from his mother's goodnight kiss, a valued ritual he depends on.

ambiguities: Geneviève (de Brabant) appears only as a figure within the magic-lantern story-within-the-story, not as a participant in the Combray household's social space; she was excluded as immaterial to local social dynamics among the actual candidate characters.

The exclusion of the narrator from his mother's goodnight kiss on evenings with company is a structural/habitual social convention rather than a single deliberate act by any one person; attributing it to the mother as source is one reasonable reading but the causal agency is diffuse (also implicating the father's disapproval of the ritual and the presence of guests generally).
